opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I love that proverb. On the surface it sounds a little morbid, but to me it's actually energizing. Life is finite and short, so you should spend it on things that genuinely matter to you and that you find joy in.

For research, I think that cuts two ways. First, it's a reminder that time is the scarcest resource you have. Science is slow. Experiments fail, biology is messy, and a single project can take years before you know whether it worked. If you only get a handful of those big swings in a career, you should be pretty deliberate about which problems you pick. I'd rather spend a decade on something ambitious that might change how we treat disease than optimize for a safe, incremental paper. Being a long time dead means the cost of not trying the hard thing is actually quite high.

The second part is the "be happy" bit, which people sometimes skip over. Demanding research can easily become grim. You're grinding, you're stressed, you're chasing the next result. But if you're not enjoying the process, the curiosity, the people you work with, the moments when something unexpected shows up in the data, then you're kind of missing the point. The best scientists I know are intense, but they're also having fun. They're playful with ideas.

So for me it's not "work yourself to death because life is short." It's more like: life is short, so pick work you'd be thrilled to spend your one life on, and then let yourself really enjoy doing it. Ambition and joy shouldn't be in tension. Ideally they feed each other.

fable-5.1.text:
I love that one. I think people hear it as a kind of carpe diem thing, go have fun, but I actually read it almost the opposite way. It's a statement about time being the only resource you really have, and the question is what you do with it.

For me, the work is the happiness. Science, or building something at Arc, is one of the few things where I get to wake up and the problem is genuinely open. Nobody knows the answer. That's a privilege. So I don't think of demanding research as the thing standing in the way of being alive. It's the most alive I feel.

But the proverb does cut the other way too. If you're going to spend your one life on hard problems, you'd better pick problems that actually matter. You're going to be a long time dead, so don't spend the short part grinding on something incremental because it's safe or because that's what the field expects. Pick the thing that, if it works, changes what's possible. That's the lens we try to apply at Arc, and honestly in my own lab. It's not "work less," it's "don't waste the hours on things you don't believe in."

And the last piece is the people. The proverb is a reminder that the day to day is it. There's no later where the real life starts after the paper comes out. So the lab culture, the collaborators, whether you're actually enjoying the arguments at the whiteboard, that's not a side thing. That is the thing.

r002.rationale: It describes the work itself as a source of happiness, but does not claim optimism or happiness gives someone the emotional capacity to persist toward long-term goals.

astra-6.text:
I take it as a reminder not to defer your whole life until the work is done. In research, there’s always another experiment, another uncertainty, another milestone. If you make happiness conditional on getting past all of that, you’re going to be waiting a long time.

That doesn’t mean avoiding demanding work. Trying to understand something difficult can be a wonderful way to spend your life. But you want to enjoy the process—the curiosity, the people you’re working with, the moments when something finally makes sense. You can take the science seriously without treating every setback as a verdict on your life.

We have a limited amount of time. To me, that’s a reason both to pursue things that matter and to appreciate being here while we do it.

I take it as a reminder not to defer all your happiness until the work succeeds. In research, there’s always another experiment, another paper, another problem. If you make your happiness conditional on reaching the end, you’re going to spend a lot of your life waiting.

That doesn’t mean avoiding demanding work. It means finding joy in the process—in being curious, in working with people you care about, in those moments when something finally makes sense. You can take the science seriously while remembering that your life is happening right now.
